intro: Castleboro is a rural townland in County Wexford, in the hills between Enniscorthy and New Ross, along the R730. In a clearing in its woods stands a tall redwood with soft red-brown bark and a wooden bench built right round its foot, so that visitors can sit with their backs against the trunk. A reader photographed it and sent it to us. We do not yet know its size, its age or who planted it, and we would like to.
meta_description: The redwood with a bench round its trunk in the woods at Castleboro, Co. Wexford, sent by a reader: where it stands and what we know.
question_meta: Castleboro's tree to see is a tall coast redwood in a woodland clearing by the R730, with a wooden bench built round its trunk.
question_answer: The tree to see at Castleboro, Co. Wexford, is the Bench Redwood: a tall coast redwood in a woodland clearing by the R730, with a wooden bench built right round its foot.
question_context: A reader sent us this tree from the clearing where it stands, in the woods at Castleboro in County Wexford. Their photograph shows a single trunk rising out of rough grass and bramble, straight and far wider than the birches and spruces around it, which breaks only high up into a dense dark crown. A wooden bench has been built right round its foot, and two visitors at the bench give the scale. The reader logged it as an Irish yew. From the photograph we read it as a coast redwood, Sequoia sempervirens. The bark is soft, fibrous and red-brown, and green shoots sprout all the way up the trunk, a habit of coast redwoods and not of yews. We have no girth, height or planting date for it, and no written source names it yet, so everything on this page comes from the photograph. We have not confirmed who owns the woods either. If you know the tree, its measurements or the history of these woods, tell us on its page and we will add it.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this tree from the woods at Castleboro in County Wexford, and the photograph makes the case for the walk on its own.

One trunk rises out of rough grass and bramble, straight as a mast and far wider than anything around it, and only high up does it break into a dense dark crown above the bare birches. Somebody thought it worth sitting with, because a wooden bench has been built right round its foot, and in the picture two visitors are standing and sitting at it, which is the best scale bar we could ask for.

The reader logged it as an Irish yew. From the photograph we read it as a coast redwood, Sequoia sempervirens. The bark is soft, fibrous and red-brown, and green shoots sprout all the way up the trunk, a habit of coast redwoods and not of yews. Tell us if you know better.

We do not know who planted it or when, and we have no girth or height for it yet. If you have measured it, or know the story of these woods, tell us here and we will add it with your figures.

Sit on the bench and look straight up the trunk.
